findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned, unverified remote script to shell
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and executes arbitrary code as root during the image build with no version pin and no integrity verification (no checksum/signature, HTTP, not HTTPS-pinned). A compromised or hijacked example.com endpoint, or a network MITM, yields root code execution and a poisoned base image; the build is also non-reproducible since the script content can change at any time.

findings.title: Curl failure silently ignored; build succeeds without install
findings.whyItBreaks: In `curl -sL ... | sh` the pipeline exit status is `sh`'s, so curl's failure is discarded. `-s` suppresses diagnostics and there is no `-f`, so a network error or HTTP 404/500 still lets curl exit 0 and feed empty/error content to `sh`; `docker build` then reports success even though the installer never ran, producing an image missing the expected tooling that only fails at runtime, conflating build failure with a legitimate value.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing into empty string in exported API
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (src/store.go:7-13) distinguishes 'key absent' (returns "", ErrMissing) from 'key present with empty value' (returns "", nil). LoadOrDefault drops the error with `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns only the string, so a legitimately stored empty value `m[k] = ""` is indistinguishable from a missing key. Because the symbol is exported, this conflated contract is the public API itself: callers cannot detect store misses to fail, retry, or apply a real default, and will silently act on "" as if it were stored data. This is the TRIGGER D public-swallow class (defined defect even with no in-repo callers).

findings.title: Keep Run synchronous or wait for spawned goroutines before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run sent one value per job on results and returned only after every send completed, so `Run(...)` returning implied "all jobs done, in job order". Now Run spawns a goroutine per job and returns immediately, so every caller that treats return as completion regresses: (a) a caller using the idiomatic pattern `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); defer close(results); Run(ctx, jobs, results)` can now close results while goroutines are still sending, panicking with "send on closed channel"; (b) a caller that reads exactly len(jobs) values after Run returns will block/hang or read results from a later call; (c) output ordering across jobs is no longer deterministic (was strictly jobs[0], jobs[1], ... order); (d) if the consumer abandons results, the spawned goroutines block on the send forever (goroutine leak), and the unused ctx cannot stop them. Note ctx was already ignored at base, so cancellation was never wired; the new defect is the loss of the completion contract and ordering, not ctx usage.

findings.title: e-to-or change grants non-admins delete rights over tenant records
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting a non-admin session with a matching tenant (isAdmin=false, session.tenantId == record.tenantId) into the changed guard: base predicate `isAdmin && tenantMatch` = false (deny), head predicate `isAdmin || tenantMatch` = true (allow). Any ordinary user in a tenant can now delete records they were previously forbidden to touch — a privilege-escalation / unauthorized-deletion authorization bypass.

findings.title: Rethrow in parseSettings catch instead of returning DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Before this change parseSettings propagated errors (JSON.parse SyntaxError, Error("bad theme"), Error("bad fontSize")), so a caller could distinguish a corrupt/invalid settings file from a legitimately-default one. Now every one of those failures is mapped to the same value as a valid default ({...DEFAULTS}) with no log and no signal. The in-repo caller updateFontSize @src/settings.ts:20 reads the result and unconditionally calls save() @src/settings.ts:22; previously a corrupt `raw` threw before save, aborting the write. Now parseSettings returns {theme:"light", fontSize:14}, updateFontSize mutates fontSize and persists {"theme":"light", fontSize:<size>}, silently overwriting the user's stored theme (and any other stored field) with defaults on any malformed input. Exported API callers additionally can no longer tell "parse failed" from "settings were already defaults", and failure-as-value is unsafe to act on. This is the same defect for in-repo and external consumers, and the exported swallow site is a present contract defect regardless of callers.

findings.title: Restore ceil in pageCount; floor undercounts pages
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount is an exported public function whose name/contract is the number of pages needed to hold totalItems items. Math.floor(totalItems / pageSize) undercounts whenever there is a remainder: pageCount(10, 3) = floor(3.33) = 3, so the last page's 1 item is dropped/unreachable. The old Math.ceil correctly returned 4. Any consumer that iterates pages 0..pageCount-1 (or renders a pager) will lose the trailing partial page.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: Report pairs builtFrom commit with artifacts from a different ref
findings.whyItBreaks: BuildReport promises `builtFrom: string` plus `artifacts: string[]` as one record of the same build (unchanged carrier, src/report.ts:6-9). Previously artifacts came from `commit = build.ref(branch)`, so builtFrom and artifacts described the same commit. The change introduces `verified = build.ref("verified")` and returns `artifactsAt(verified)` while `builtFrom` stays the branch commit. Any consumer that reads `builtFrom` to identify the source of `artifacts` (e.g. publishing/deploying the reported artifacts) now acts on artifacts that may belong to a different ref than the reported one, with no field indicating the mismatch. This is a silent internal inconsistency on the exported public function.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps results at `limit`
findings.whyItBreaks: Base implementation was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body builds `sorted` then returns it directly without `.slice(0, limit)`, so `recentEntries(all, n)` now returns ALL of `all` (newest-first) for any n > 0 instead of at most n. The doc comment on line 1 ('Returns at most `limit` entries') still promises the cap. This is not just an unused export: renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and then copies into a fixed `new Array<string>(20)` (line 10) via `out[i] = page[i]` (line 11). With page.length > 20 the loop writes past index 20, growing `out` and returning a feed larger than the intended 20-entry page — a user-facing regression in the rendered feed size/ordering contract.

findings.title: monthRange end excludes the last day of the month
findings.whyItBreaks: Date.UTC(year, month, 0) resolves to 00:00 UTC of the LAST day of the month (e.g. month=1/2024 -> Jan 31 2024T00:00Z), not the exclusive start of the next month. contains() at src/lib/date-range.ts:32 uses an exclusive bound (t < range.end.getTime()), so any timestamp on the last day of the month fails the range test. The monthly consumer at src/reports/monthly.ts:17 filters invoices with `contains(range, inv.issuedAt)`, so every invoice issued on the last day of the month is dropped before totals are summed at src/reports/monthly.ts:19, producing a wrong invoiceCount/totalCents. Those values flow unchanged into the CSV row at src/reports/export.ts:9-10, so the exported report silently undercounts a full day of revenue every month. Old code (Date.UTC(year, month, 1) = exclusive start of next month) was correct, so this is a regression.

facts.meaning: monthRange's end is now day 0 of the following month (the requested month's last day at midnight) instead of the first day of the next month.
Records on the last day of a month fall outside the half-open range and are omitted from monthly totals.

findings.title: Keep entry-count header consistent with filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff rebuilds `rows` from `live` (non-stale entries only), but line 22 still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` with the unfiltered array length. The emitted `# entry-count:` header therefore advertises a count that contradicts the number of listed rows whenever any entry has stale=true (e.g. 2 entries with 1 stale prints `# entry-count: 2` followed by 1 row). A consumer parsing the header to size/validate the entry list receives inconsistent data, where before this change the count and rows always agreed.

findings.title: Restore execute: unconditional throw breaks exported core path
findings.whyItBreaks: The body of `execute(input: string): string` was changed from `return input.toUpperCase();` to `throw new Error("always fails");`. The function is the only exported/public symbol in the repo (src/runner.ts:1) and its signature promises a `string` return, but it now always throws before returning. Every caller and every future caller of the public API gets an exception instead of a value; there is no input for which the function can succeed, so the core path is completely unusable (contract drift: the unchanged `: string` carrier promises a result the body never produces).

findings.title: Viewer gate makes handle()'s read-only branch unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false for role === "viewer" (src/handler.ts:18) before handle() can reach its intended viewer behavior. handle() still routes viewers to "read-only" at src/handler.ts:25, but that line is now dead: any active viewer with attempts < 5 previously passed isEligible and got "read-only"; it now short-circuits at src/handler.ts:24 to "rejected". The changed predicate therefore rejects an action (read-only processing of viewers) that handle() itself deems legitimately approvable, breaking the viewer workflow and silently orphaning the "read-only" branch.

findings.title: Payment gate over-blocks saving an unpaid draft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `order.payment === "paid"` makes saveDraft reject the normal draft case: substituting state="draft", payment="missing" yields `true && false` = false, so saveDraft now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Requiring payment to persist a draft is not a legitimate precondition for that action, so saveDraft no longer works for unpaid drafts — the exact case a draft represents.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns stable's files under requested channel/commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changed `files: repo.filesAt(head)` to `files: repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")`, but the returned `commit` (line 16) and `channel` (line 17) are still derived from the requested `channel`. The resulting Snapshot is internally inconsistent: for any channel != "stable" the files come from the stable ref while commit/channel claim the requested ref. Callers that publish or persist `snapshot.files` keyed by `snapshot.channel`/`snapshot.commit` will ship the wrong revision's content labeled as the requested channel (verified against base 4f2b05e where files came from `head`).

findings.title: Honor new `limit` parameter in build()
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature now promises a `limit` cap on the returned list (default 10), but the body still hardcodes `max_count = 10` (src/builder.py:2) and never reads `limit`. A caller invoking e.g. `build('p', limit=3)` expects 3 items under the advertised contract but receives 10, silently violating the cap the parameter exists to provide.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int or rename it
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename changes the carrier from the neutral `read_int` to `parse_positive_int`, which promises the result is validated as positive. The body `return int(value)` performs no range check, so `parse_positive_int(-5)` returns -5. `charge()` at line 6 forwards the amount straight into `n * 100` with no validation of its own, so a negative or zero amount silently produces a negative/zero charge instead of being rejected. The name now lies about a contract that external callers will trust.

findings.title: apply_values mutates caller's DataFrame instead of returning a copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `result = df.copy()` was the only thing preventing caller data mutation. `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` now writes through to the caller's DataFrame, so any caller that reuses `df` after `apply_values(df, mapping)` (e.g. reads the original values, calls the function twice, or compares before/after) silently observes modified data. Previously `apply_values` returned a transformed copy and left the argument untouched.

findings.title: CI workflow moved out of .github/workflows disables all CI
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff is a pure rename of .github/workflows/ci.yml to docs/ci.md (similarity 100%). GitHub Actions only discovers workflow files under .github/workflows/, so after this change no CI runs on push or pull_request. The workflow's triggers (`on: push` / `on: pull_request`) and steps (`npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm test`) are now inert documentation, and README.md:3's claim "CI runs lint and tests on every push" is now false. A bad merge that breaks lint/tests would land on main with no gate.

findings.title: Remove `dbg!(items)`; it moves `items` and breaks compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: std's `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, binding the scrutinee by value. `items` is `Vec<String>` (non-Copy), so `dbg!(items)` moves it into the macro's temporary, which is then dropped at the end of the statement. Line 3 `let total = items.len();` therefore uses a moved value, producing `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: items` — the crate fails to build. As a secondary effect, `dbg!` writes `items` to stderr unconditionally (it is not stripped in release builds), leaking input contents into logs even if the move were avoided.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against the reported fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Changeset contract states fromRevision is 'Revision the changed paths were computed against' and that 'Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision' (src/changeset.ts:7-9). After the change, fromRevision is still store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 14/17) but changedPaths is now store.readChangedPaths(latest) (line 18). The returned diff no longer corresponds to the revision it is paired with, so any consumer that replays/applies changedPaths on top of fromRevision operates on a mismatched revision — the path set is from "latest" while the base is the pinned tag, producing an incorrect replay (wrong/extra/missing files). Previously both fields derived from the same resolved revision, so the invariant held.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql for email->contact_email rename
findings.whyItBreaks: migrations/0001_init.sql created users.email and src/query.sql:1 selects `email` from users. This new migration renames that column to `contact_email` but no consumer is updated, so after migrations run, `SELECT email FROM users` fails with "column email does not exist" — the repo's only read path (and any external consumer of the renamed column) is broken by the upgrade.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: The env lookup is replaced by a literal credential ("bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0"). This commits a live-looking billing secret to the repository: anyone with read access to the source/history gets a working key, it cannot be rotated or scoped per environment, and every deployment (dev/staging/prod) now authenticates as the same principal. Supply-chain/secret-leak defect that ships the moment this merges, and secrets in git history persist even after removal.

findings.title: Inverted admin check lets non-admins purge and blocks admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required `user.isAdmin && project.archived` to delete. The new guard `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden";` rejects exactly the privileged user, so combined with `if (!project.archived) return "forbidden";` the only path reaching `db.delete(project.id)` is a NON-admin acting on an archived project. This is a privilege-escalation / authorization bypass: regular users gain destructive purge capability, and the legitimate admin purge path is permanently blocked.

findings.title: startup() now crashes on missing config instead of using defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when the config path does not exist (app/config.py:5-7). The removed guard substituted {"workers": 1, "region": "us-east-1"}, so startup(path) previously returned 1 for a missing/absent config. After the change, settings stays None and `int(settings["workers"])` raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`, so any caller that starts up without a config file (fresh install, unmounted volume, optional config) now crashes instead of booting with the documented default. Concrete traced consumer: `settings=None → startup @app/config.py:14 → subscription branch taken → TypeError raised, no workers value returned`.

findings.title: Return gateway error instead of logging it and returning nil
findings.whyItBreaks: Charge's contract is `func Charge(...) error`, but on a failed submit it now logs the error and falls through to `return nil` (pay/charge.go:17-19). The change was `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` -> `log.Printf(...)`. Any caller that checks the returned error (the only signal it has) will treat a failed/declined/dropped charge as success, fulfilling the order or recording payment without the charge actually happening. This is an exported (public) function, so the swallowed-failure contract is the defect itself even with no in-repo caller yet.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in settings cache key (cross-tenant leak)
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key changed from `${tenantId}:${name}` to `settings:${name}`, dropping tenant scoping. `store.fetch(tenantId, name)` still reads per-tenant data, but the cached result is now stored/looked up by name alone. The second tenant to request the same setting name gets a cache HIT and receives the first tenant's value verbatim (`if (hit !== undefined) return hit;`), so tenant B observes tenant A's configuration — a cross-tenant data leak and wrong-config bug on a live read path.

findings.title: async reserve() allows concurrent oversell of the last unit
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version did the read-check-write synchronously (this.stock.set was atomic within the single-threaded run). The new version yields at line 17 `await this.store.save(...)`, so the check at line 16 and the mutation at line 18 are no longer contiguous. Two concurrent reserve('x') calls when one unit remains both read remaining=1, both pass `remaining <= 0`, both persist 0 and both `this.stock.set(sku, 0)` and return true: two reservations succeed for one unit and the persistent store is written the same value twice (lost update). The mutation must not be separated from the guard by an await, or needs an in-flight lock/atomic op.

findings.title: backoff unit change not applied to retry call site (1000x longer sleeps)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) and both call sites converted with *1000. This diff changes backoff() to return milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and drops the *1000 only in src/net/poll.ts. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still computes `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)` on the now-millisecond value, so the sleep is 1000x too large: attempt 0 yields 2**0*1000*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1000 ms, and attempt >=5 yields the cap 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of the previous 30 s. Failed jobs become effectively hung on every retry.

findings.title: Save silently discards file Close error on success path
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the success path returned f.Close()'s error (base line 24), so a write-back failure surfaced at close (e.g. ENOSPC/EDQUOT on NFS, delayed disk-full) was reported to callers. The new code returns only w.Flush() and closes via `defer f.Close()`, whose error is dropped. w.Flush() only pushes buffered bytes into the OS; the durable-write error for a written file commonly surfaces on Close, so Save can now return nil even though data was not fully persisted. This is an exported function, so the error-propagation contract itself regressed for every caller.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation iterated the half-open window with range(start, end) (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)), yielding every row in the page. The refactor keeps the same end bound from _window_bounds (also documented as half-open [start,end)) but iterates range(start, end - 1), so the last row of every page is omitted. For a full page (end == start+page_size) only page_size-1 rows are returned; for the final partial page the last row of the dataset is never returned, and a last page with a single remaining row returns an empty list. render_page therefore emits shorter, mis-numbered pages and summarize silently omits the dataset's final row.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired cache entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now `get` returns the value only when the entry is already expired (age > ttlMs) and falls through to `entries.delete` + `null` when the entry is still fresh. Every caller that relied on the TTL as a freshness guarantee now receives stale data (potentially indefinitely-reused expired values) while valid entries are dropped on first read.

findings.title: pruneDone skips entries: splice during forEach leaves done jobs in the array
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while `forEach` advances its index shifts the array under the iterator, so any two consecutive `done` jobs cause the second to be skipped and the array is left containing a done job. The old `jobs.filter((job) => !job.done)` removed every done job; the new body fails its own contract of pruning done jobs.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates and returns the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously returned a new filtered array and left the input untouched. The rewritten body splices the caller's `jobs` array and returns that same reference, so any caller that keeps using its original list (or checks length/identity) sees it silently truncated — a dropped defensive copy that changes observable behavior for existing callers.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard means an empty array now computes `0 / 0`, returning NaN. NaN silently poisons any downstream arithmetic or comparison (sums become NaN, `x > y` comparisons are always false, aggregations/reports render NaN), so callers can no longer distinguish 'no rows' from a broken sum. The exported function's prior contract (empty -> 0) is now violated.

findings.title: busiest mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array in place. Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver, so any code holding a reference to the passed array (e.g. rendering 'rows' in their original order, reusing the list for pagination/export, or relying on a stable identity/order elsewhere) now observes a reordered array as an unexpected side effect. This is dropped defensive-copy behavior, a real caller-visible regression independent of the return value.

findings.title: rankScores uses lexicographic sort, returning wrong top players
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator sorts by string coercion, not magnitude. The base revision used `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` (true numeric descending). The new `scores.sort(); scores.reverse();` orders scores lexicographically, so `cutoff = scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` at line 15 is often the wrong threshold. Concretely, with players [{name:'a',score:4},{name:'b',score:30},{name:'c',score:20}] and n=1: lexicographic asc = [20,30,4] ("20"<"30"<"4"), reversed = [4,30,20], cutoff = 4, so `p.score >= 4` keeps every player and `slice(0,1)` returns the first in input order ('a', score 4) instead of the true maximum ('b', score 30). The exposed `formatBoard` (line 19-22) renders this incorrect ranking directly.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates the 401/200 decision in handle() (app/webhook.py:14) on a secret-derived MAC, but the diff replaces the constant-time hmac.compare_digest with Python's `==`. str.__eq__ short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest an attacker guessed. An attacker who can submit requests and measure latency can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and forge payloads that pass handle(), turning the auth gate into a bypass.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction break atomic transfer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction():`, so a failure rolled back the whole transfer. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the `with` block (line 23); `_apply_balances` runs after the block on line 24, in autocommit/no-transaction scope. The ledger row is committed first, then the two balance UPDATEs run non-atomically. If the credit UPDATE raises (or the process dies between the two UPDATEs), the ledger records the transfer and the debit may already be applied while the recipient is never credited — persisted state diverges and funds are silently lost, with no rollback path.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on UTC date parts to avoid timezone-dependent days
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation read getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, but the new body reads getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which resolve in the host's local timezone. The same instant now maps to different billing days depending on the server's TZ and rolls over at local midnight rather than UTC midnight. Example: on a UTC+8 host, new Date('2026-09-28T20:00:00Z') returns '2026-09-29' at head but '2026-09-28' at base; hosts in different zones disagree about the same event, so entries near the boundary are split into, or attributed to, the wrong billing period. sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the same instability.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key to prevent cross-tenant cache collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key dropped the tenant namespace: `const key = account;` while the module-level `memo` Map is shared across all tenants. readProfile("tenantB", "alice", ...) hits the entry previously written by readProfile("tenantA", "alice", ...) and returns tenantA's Profile (including `tenant: "tenantA"`) without calling fetchProfile. Any account name that exists under more than one tenant yields wrong data and leaks another tenant's profile; `if (cached) return cached;` (line 16) short-circuits before the tenant-scoped fetch on line 17.

findings.title: Stop swallowing missing-key error in exported load()
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is an exported API that previously signaled a missing key by throwing `missing: <key>`. The new `catch { return "" }` maps that failure to the default "". Because the store is a `Map<string, string>`, "" is a legal value (`store.set(k, "")`), so callers can no longer distinguish 'key absent' from 'key present with empty value'. Any consumer of `load`/`loadAll` that treats "" as data — persisting it, rendering it, or reporting it as a real result — will now silently act on a value that was never stored, and genuine lookup failures are lost with no log or rethrow. Previously the error reached the caller's own try/catch; now that point receives a plausible-looking string instead.

findings.title: Rename exported config field timeoutMs to timeout breaks callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported `Config` dropped `timeoutMs` and added `timeout`, and `retry` now reads `config.timeout` (line 8). Any existing consumer that still passes `{ timeoutMs: ... }` gets `config.timeout === undefined`, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined === NaN` and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` is always false — the deadline short-circuit never fires and the loop runs to `maxAttempts` regardless of the intended time budget. TypeScript consumers additionally fail to compile (`timeout` required, `timeoutMs` no longer exists), so this is a breaking change with a silent-failure mode for JS callers.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows failure and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: The added public function catches every thrown error with `catch { continue; }` (line 27) and, once all attempts are exhausted, falls off the end and returns `undefined`. Callers cannot distinguish "all attempts failed" from "succeeded", and the last error is discarded entirely (not even re-thrown or logged), so an eventual caller is forced to treat exhaustion as success — the classic persist/report-the-fallback hazard.

findings.title: Numeric value yields "len=undefined"; input no longer shows value
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop type now explicitly promises numbers are accepted (`value: string | number` @src/components/Field.tsx:2), but the body computes `value.length` (@src/components/Field.tsx:6). A `string | number` union has no `length`, so a number (e.g. `42`) produces `undefined` and the input renders the literal text `len=undefined` instead of the value. Additionally `defaultValue` was changed from `value` to `label` (@src/components/Field.tsx:7), so even string callers no longer see their real value in the input, only `len=<n>` — the field's displayed content is wrong for every consumer, and observably broken for the newly-permitted numeric case.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step binds `TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` into the step environment and interpolates it into `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, printing the credential on the runner. GitHub's log masking is best-effort and does not protect against transformed/substring output (encoding, splitting, multi-line values, tool-formatted output), and any log export, artifact, or downstream log consumer receives the plaintext secret, enabling credential theft and unauthorized deploys. This step also performs no deploy action, so it adds only leak risk.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; large diffs now abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 (1 MiB), down from the removed 64 MiB. git() also runs the full patch command `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) and `git diff --name-only` (line 57), whose combined output routinely exceeds 1 MiB on larger PRs. When stdout exceeds maxBuffer, Node kills the child and sets res.error=ENOBUFS with res.status=null, so `res.status !== 0` is true at line 38 and runGithub throws; its catch posts a failing check-run ('Review errored and did NOT pass this PR') and sets exitCode=1. The 64 MiB budget on the sibling gh()/ghText() calls (lines 19, 29) was intentionally kept, showing the removal is an accidental regression, not a deliberate tighter limit.

findings.title: Keep -s read-only so spawned review codex cannot write the repo
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `codex exec` was pinned to the read-only sandbox regardless of ambient config. Now `-s` is absent, so the sandbox comes from config/permission-profile resolution: for a project with a recorded trust decision (codex's default builtin profile for trusted/untrusted projects) the effective policy is `workspace-write`, which permits `spawnSync`'s cwd (opts.repoPath = the repo under review) to be created/modified. Verified empirically with codex-cli 0.157.1: a rollout from `codex exec` in this repo records `"sandbox_policy":{"type":"workspace-write",...}` while the same command in a dir with no trust entry records `"sandbox_policy":{"type":"read-only"}`, and `codex debug prompt-input` reports `sandbox_mode is workspace-write` here vs `read-only` elsewhere. `codex exec` also forces `approval_policy = never`, so those writes are auto-approved and never surfaced to the caller. Net effect: the review subprocess (which ingests untrusted PR content/diffs) is no longer prevented from writing to the repository it is reviewing, and a user config pinning a broader `sandbox_mode`/permission profile widens it further.

findings.title: Diff PR against base tip/HEAD, not merge-base+headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, the patch was `git diff <merge-base(baseSha, headSha)> <headSha>` (three-dot, PR-only changes) and changedFiles used the same merge base. It is now `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)`. Two concrete breakages: (1) `baseSha` is the base-branch tip, so a two-dot diff includes every commit that landed on the base branch after the PR forked — those appear as deletions of code the PR never touched — and the review model/finding filter now operates on non-PR content; (2) the diff uses the literal local `HEAD` instead of the env-provided `headSha`, so the patch can describe a different commit than the one the review/check is anchored to via `commit_id` (src/adapters/github.ts:85) and `head_sha` (src/adapters/github.ts:124), which still use `headSha`. changedPaths (src/adapters/github.ts:141) also becomes polluted, so inline comments (src/adapters/github.ts:61) can target lines absent from the real PR diff.

findings.title: String replaceValue re-enables $-pattern corruption of prompt input
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only treats the replacement as literal when it is a function; a string replacement applies the GetSubstitution `$` grammar ($$ -> $, $& -> matched text, $` -> prefix, $' -> suffix). At line 33 `bundle.patch` (raw PR diff text) is inserted as a plain string, so any `$` sequence in the diff is rewritten: `$$` collapses to `$`, and `$&`, `` $` `` or `$'` re-inject the placeholder/preceding/following prompt text into the critic prompt. Lines 25 and 32 are equally affected because JSON.stringify(bundle) contains `bundle.patch` and candidate text. Diffs of shell, sed/awk, make, Perl or JS/TS regex code routinely contain these sequences, so the critic silently reviews mangled or duplicated content (and an attacker-authored patch can steer that rewrite), producing wrong or missed findings with no error surfaced. The base code passed `() =>` thunks precisely to keep the value literal.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed findings into fake P1 findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Every validation that previously rejected bad model output is gone and replaced with silent defaults: invalid severity becomes "P1" (line 98), missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (line 99), invalid category becomes "bug" (line 100-102), missing file is kept as "" (line 103) instead of a required non-empty path, and lineStart/lineEnd default to 0/NaN with no finite/positive check (lines 104-105). A malformed finding is therefore returned as a plausible, high-severity Finding pointing at an empty file and line 0. Callers can no longer distinguish 'model returned garbage' from 'model found a real P1 bug', so corrupt output is persisted/reported as genuine findings and can flip a review verdict.

findings.title: normalizeReview dropped strict flag and no longer drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature changed from normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) to normalizeReview(raw) (line 113) and the lenient branch that caught per-finding errors and filtered them out is replaced by a bare raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (line 131). Combined with the unvalidated normalizeFinding, this removes both behaviors callers could rely on: strict throw-on-malformed AND lenient drop-malformed. A caller passing strict=false previously received only well-formed findings; it now receives every malformed entry coerced into a default-valued finding, so filtering silently stops working with no error.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for `gh pr view` in pre-checkout ref step
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step is the first step of the job and runs before `actions/checkout` (.github/workflows/review.yml:42), so the workspace working directory is not a git repository and has no `origin` remote. `gh` can only resolve the target repo from `-R`/`GH_REPO` or the cwd git remote; it does NOT fall back to `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified locally: in a non-git dir, `gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository` even with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set). This branch is the one taken on `workflow_dispatch` (`EVENT_HEAD` is empty because `github.event.pull_request` is null there), i.e. the manual PR-number trigger the file explicitly documents at lines 9-12. Result: `gh` errors, and because the failure is inside `echo "$(...)"` under `bash -e`, the step still exits 0 and writes `head=`/`base=` (empty) to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, so the following checkout gets an empty `ref` and silently checks out the default ref rather than failing loudly.

findings.title: Stop normalizeReview from swallowing malformed-output errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Base normalizeReview threw on malformed model output (`!raw || typeof raw !== 'object'`, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks at base lines 115-131), so a caller could detect bad output and retry/fail. The new body instead coerces every defect into a default: non-object/empty input now returns `{ summary: '', findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }`, a nil/empty value that is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a real 'no issues' review. A consumer that renders or acts on this result sees ''/[] and reports a clean pass instead of a parse failure, silently masking garbage LLM output. Because `normalizeReview` is exported, every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value — the false-empty value flows into a verdict/approval decision.

findings.title: Restore PR head/base resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On a workflow_dispatch run the event payload has no pull_request object, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 29) is empty and checkout falls back to `github.ref` — the branch selected/default branch, not the PR head. Likewise PR_BASE_SHA (line 45) and PR_HEAD_SHA (line 46) become empty strings. The deleted "Resolve PR refs" step existed precisely for this case: its else-branch ran `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid` to resolve the real SHAs. The workflow still advertises the manual path (on.workflow_dispatch with required `pr_number` input at lines 10-14, and the `if:` at line 24 still permits it), so the manual trigger now reviews the wrong commit or fails instead of reviewing the requested PR.

findings.title: Removing maxBuffer caps git diff output at 1 MiB, failing large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024 * 1024 (1 MiB). This line previously raised it to 64 MiB. The `patch` payload for the whole review is produced by `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` at src/adapters/local.ts:100 and is stored directly into the bundle at src/adapters/local.ts:123, so it is the full PR diff. When that diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync terminates the child with ENOBUFS, leaving `res.status` non-zero/null, so the guard at src/adapters/local.ts:12 throws `git diff ... failed:` and the entire review fails. Large PRs that previously reviewed fine (up to 64 MiB) now cannot run at all; if the platform instead truncated stdout, the reviewer would silently receive an incomplete diff. Either outcome is a regression from the removed 64 MiB limit, and it is inconsistent with `gh()` at src/adapters/local.ts:33-37, which still sets 64 MiB.

findings.title: Review-error path downgraded from failing check to non-blocking neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: On the catch path the check run is now posted with conclusion "neutral" (previously "failure"). GitHub treats neutral (like skipped) as a non-failing conclusion for required status checks, so a PR whose review never completed is no longer blocked by the "Needlefish" check. This directly contradicts the summary still shipped on that same call (`Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.`), turning the gate fail-open: the reviewer crashes (e.g. `gh`/`git` failure, model error) and the PR becomes mergeable with zero review. Note `postCheck`'s conclusion union still admits "failure" and the success path still uses `changes_requested → "failure"`, so the error path should keep failing closed.

findings.title: Keep PR code as data; don't run it as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the workflow checked out the untrusted PR head to `target` as read-only data and installed/ran the tool from a second checkout of `frankekn/needlefish@main` (trusted). This diff deletes that second checkout and the `working-directory: needlefish`, so `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (lines 49-59) now execute code contained in the PR head itself. The removed comment documented the exact protection being dropped: 'This prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' The repo-level guard at line 24 only limits automatic runs to same-repo PRs, but any insider/compromised account with branch-push rights qualifies, and a PR that edits `src/cli.ts` (or adds an npm install/postinstall hook, now run from the PR's lockfile) will be judged by its own modified reviewer and run arbitrary commands on the self-hosted runner holding a `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` `GITHUB_TOKEN`. This is a real escalation because pre-change no PR-controlled code was ever executed.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently downgrades non-uppercase severities to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior body computed `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the membership test, so "p1", " p1 ", or "P1 " were accepted and preserved. The new body tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` against the raw value, so any non-canonical casing/whitespace (e.g. "p1") now fails the check and falls to the fallback, which this same diff lowered from "P1" to "P3". Result: a case-variant P0/P1 finding is silently reclassified as P3 (lowest), which for a review gate means a blocking finding can be reported as non-blocking. The removed normalization also contradicts the exported function's name/purpose (contract drift), and line 132 (`raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)`) stores the un-normalized severity directly.

findings.title: Re-exposes GitHub tokens to spawned codex process
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code built `const env = { ...process.env }`, deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed `env` to spawnSync. This PR removes both the sanitized copy and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default of inheriting the full `process.env`. The codex child (run with `exec`, which can execute shell commands and launch subprocesses/MCP servers) now receives GitHub credentials that were previously intentionally withheld, re-introducing secret exposure/privilege for any agent-initiated action in the child.

findings.title: Restore fork guard before running untrusted PRs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow triggers on `pull_request` (line 7-9), which fires for PRs from forks. The removed line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing fork PRs from running here. With it gone, the `review` job now runs unconditionally on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18). It then checks out the PR head (lines 20-24), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, which executes the PR's install/lifecycle scripts), and runs `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) — i.e. arbitrary PR-authored code — on the self-hosted machine. Even though GitHub withholds repo secrets and downgrades `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only for forked `pull_request` runs, executing untrusted fork code on self-hosted infrastructure is the well-known critical risk: an attacker fork PR can compromise the persistent runner, exfiltrate anything reachable on that host, plant persistence, and pivot into the internal network. The guard is the standard documented mitigation for exactly this, and its removal is a supply-chain/security regression.

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs now silently ignores an explicit 0 value
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported helper previously accepted any finite non-negative duration (`parsed >= 0`) but now rejects 0 (`parsed > 0`), so a valid, intentional configuration is silently replaced by the fallback. Substitution: value="0" -> readRunnerDurationMs returns the fallback, not 0. On the live config path, `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` is read at src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-6 and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` at src/shared/runner-process.ts:7-10; with 0 previously honored, the operator's "no grace, escalate immediately" setting is dropped and RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS/RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS silently become 5000/2000. On a timeout path the runner now waits up to 5000ms before SIGKILL and 2000ms before giving up (src/shared/runner-process.ts:120-124) instead of escalating immediately. This is a behavior regression on a config value that the old code explicitly supported, not merely a rejected invalid input.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so all changed files are deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block built `covered` from the selected hotspots and pushed a tail-coverage hotspot for every changed file not in it, so no changed file could be silently skipped. After `hotspots = sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6), any changed file not mapped to a surface, and any file belonging to a hotspot dropped by the slice, is now never deep-reviewed. Nothing records the omission (residual_risks is also hardcoded to [] at line 113), so reviewLarge can return a passing verdict while never examining part of the diff.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution and focus in mapBundle
findings.whyItBreaks: The hunk deleted the only `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep-prompt chain, and the earlier hunk removed `focus: bundle.focus` (plus `deep`) from `mapBundle`. `prompts/deep.md` still contains `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)`, and `prompts/map.md` still says to rank surfaces higher when the bundle's `focus` field is set. On the large-PR path (patch > 30000 chars or > 10 changed files) this now sends the literal token `{{FOCUS}}` to the model and the user's `--focus <text>` argument is silently ignored, so focused review no longer works for large PRs even though the CLI flag and Bundle.focus still exist.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit 60 seconds ("60s" / "1m 60s")
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds is Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000), which can round up to 60 while minutes was already fixed by Math.floor. ms=59999 -> minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 -> "60s"; ms=119500 -> minutes=1, seconds=round(59.5)=60 -> "1m 60s". The previous implementation derived seconds from rounded total seconds (totalSeconds % 60), which could never reach 60. These strings are rendered into the review markdown (render.ts:75, render.ts:80).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing, while the exported function name and the thrown message (`${label} requires a positive integer`) still promise strict positivity. This is the sole validation this helper performs, and it is exported (public contract), so any caller using it to reject non-positive counts/limits/timeouts will now let 0 through, e.g. a zero timeout (immediate abort), a zero concurrency/page/count (no work, division by zero downstream), or a zero limit that bypasses the intended guard. Zero was previously rejected, so this is a contract/validation regression, not just a style change.
